source.title: First Aid Basics
source.attribution: A Reborn guide in our own words, drawing on St John Ambulance and the NHS.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. References: St John Ambulance, First aid advice, https://www.sja.org.uk/first-aid-advice/; St John Ambulance, CPR, https://www.sja.org.uk/first-aid-advice/cpr/; St John Ambulance, Choking, https://www.sja.org.uk/first-aid-advice/choking/; St John Ambulance, Severe bleeding, https://www.sja.org.uk/first-aid-advice/severe-bleeding/; St John Ambulance, Burns and scalds, https://www.sja.org.uk/first-aid-advice/burns-and-scalds/; NHS, Stroke symptoms, https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/stroke/symptoms/

cards.title: Keep yourself safe and call for help first
cards.body:
In an emergency, your first job is to make sure you do not become a second casualty. Look for danger such as traffic, fire, electricity, deep water or violence before you go near someone. If it is not safe, keep back and call for help.

Call your local emergency number as early as possible, or ask someone else to. Say where you are, what happened and how many people are hurt. Put the phone on speaker so the call handler can guide you while you help.

This guide covers the basics only. The best way to be ready is to take a proper hands-on first-aid course.
cards.apply_it: Save your local emergency number in your phone and find out where your nearest first-aid course runs.

quiz.question: What should you check before approaching an injured person?
options: That it is safe for you to approach
quiz.explanation: Checking for danger first protects you, so you can help instead of becoming another casualty.

cards.title: Check if they respond and are breathing normally
cards.body:
Once it is safe, kneel beside the person. Gently shake their shoulders and ask loudly, "Can you hear me? Open your eyes." If they respond, keep them still, ask what happened and call for help if needed.

If they do not respond, open their airway: place one hand on their forehead, tilt the head back gently, and lift the chin with two fingertips. Then look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than ten seconds.

Occasional gasps are not normal breathing. If they are unresponsive and not breathing normally, call your local emergency number and start CPR.
cards.apply_it: Practise the head tilt and chin lift on a willing friend so the movement feels familiar.

quiz.question: Someone is unresponsive and only making occasional gasps. What does that mean?
options: Treat it as not breathing normally and start CPR
quiz.explanation: Occasional gasps are not normal breathing. Call for help and start CPR.

cards.title: Use the recovery position for someone breathing but unresponsive
cards.body:
If a person is unresponsive but breathing normally, and you do not suspect a serious back or neck injury, place them on their side in the recovery position. This keeps the airway open and lets vomit drain out instead of choking them.

Kneel beside them. Place the arm nearest you at a right angle, palm up. Bring the far arm across their chest and hold the back of that hand against their cheek. Bend the far knee up, then pull on it to roll them towards you onto their side. Tilt the head back slightly to keep the airway open.

Call for help and keep checking their breathing until it arrives.
cards.apply_it: Watch a recovery-position video from a recognised first-aid organisation and practise with a family member.

quiz.question: Why is the recovery position used?
options: To keep the airway open and let fluids drain
quiz.explanation: Lying on the side keeps the airway clear and prevents choking on vomit.

cards.title: Know the basics of CPR for adults
cards.body:
If an adult is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call your local emergency number and start CPR. Ask someone to find a defibrillator (AED) if one is nearby.

Place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, put your other hand on top and lock your fingers. With straight arms, press down hard and fast, about 5 to 6 centimetres deep, at 100 to 120 compressions a minute. Let the chest come back up each time. If you are trained, you can give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions; if not, keep doing chest compressions only.

When the defibrillator arrives, switch it on and follow its spoken instructions.
cards.apply_it: Learn a song with about 100 to 120 beats a minute to help keep pace, and look for a CPR class near you.

quiz.question: What should you do if you're not trained to give rescue breaths?
quiz.explanation: Hands-only CPR is far better than nothing. Keep pushing hard and fast until help or a defibrillator arrives.

cards.title: Help an adult who is choking
cards.body:
If someone can still cough, speak or breathe, encourage them to keep coughing, as this is often enough to clear the blockage.

If they cannot cough, speak or breathe, act fast. Help them lean forward and give up to five sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. Check their mouth after each one. If that fails, stand behind them, place a fist just above the belly button, grab it with your other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards up to five times.

If it still has not cleared, call your local emergency number and keep repeating the cycle. If they become unresponsive, start CPR. Anyone given abdominal thrusts should be checked by a doctor.
cards.apply_it: Learn the two steps: five back blows, then five abdominal thrusts. Say them out loud once to fix them in memory.

quiz.question: What should you do first if a choking adult can still cough?
quiz.explanation: Coughing is the body's best tool. Only move to back blows and thrusts if coughing isn't working.

cards.title: Stop severe bleeding with firm pressure
cards.body:
Heavy bleeding can become life-threatening quickly, so act straight away. Wear gloves if you have them. Press firmly on the wound with a clean pad or cloth and keep pressing. If something is stuck in the wound, leave it in and press around it instead.

Call your local emergency number, or get someone else to. Help the person lie down. Once you can, bandage the pad firmly in place, but not so tight that it cuts off blood flow beyond it.

If blood soaks through, put another pad on top and keep pressing rather than removing the first one. Watch for signs of shock while you wait.
cards.apply_it: Check that your home has clean dressings and gloves, and know where they are kept.

quiz.question: What should you do if an object is stuck in a wound?
options: Leave it in and press around it
quiz.explanation: Removing an embedded object can make bleeding worse. Leave it in and apply pressure around it.

cards.title: Cool a burn with running water for 20 minutes
cards.body:
For a burn or scald, cool it under cool or lukewarm running water for at least 20 minutes as soon as possible. This reduces pain and damage. Remove rings, watches or clothing near the burn unless they are stuck to the skin.

After cooling, cover it loosely with cling film laid on in strips, or a clean plastic bag for a hand, to protect it from infection. Do not use ice, butter, creams or toothpaste, and do not burst blisters.

Get medical help for burns that are large, deep, on the face, hands, feet or genitals, caused by chemicals or electricity, or on a child or older person.
cards.apply_it: Tell your household the 20-minute rule today so everyone knows what to do if someone gets burned.

quiz.question: Which is the right first step for a burn?
options: Cool it under running water for at least 20 minutes
quiz.explanation: Cool running water for at least 20 minutes is the most helpful first step. Ice, butter and creams can cause harm.

cards.title: Spot and treat shock
cards.body:
Shock here means a medical emergency where not enough blood is reaching vital organs, often after heavy bleeding, severe burns or a serious injury. Signs include pale, cold, clammy skin, a fast and then weak pulse, fast shallow breathing, dizziness, feeling sick, and confusion or restlessness.

Treat any cause you can, such as bleeding. Call your local emergency number and say you think it is shock. Help the person lie down and, if they have no leg, hip or pelvis injury, raise and support their legs. Loosen tight clothing and keep them warm with a coat or blanket.

Stay with them, reassure them and watch their breathing.
cards.apply_it: Memorise three signs of shock: pale clammy skin, fast breathing and a fast, weak pulse.

quiz.question: When should you NOT raise the legs of someone in shock?
options: When a leg, hip or pelvis injury is suspected
quiz.explanation: Raising the legs helps blood flow, but not if it could worsen a leg, hip or pelvis injury.

cards.title: Keep a suspected broken bone still
cards.body:
Signs of a broken bone include pain, swelling, bruising, a limb that looks bent or shorter, and difficulty moving it. If you are unsure, treat it as a break.

Ask the person to keep still and support the injured part in the most comfortable position, using your hands, padding or rolled clothing. Do not try to straighten it. A sling can support an arm. If bone is showing through the skin, cover the wound with a clean dressing and press around it, not on the bone.

Call your local emergency number for serious breaks, such as a thigh, back, neck or pelvis, or if bone is visible. Watch for shock.
cards.apply_it: Practise making a simple arm sling from a scarf or triangular bandage.

quiz.question: What should you avoid doing with a suspected broken limb?
quiz.explanation: Moving or straightening a broken bone can cause more damage. Support it as it is and get help.

cards.title: Protect someone having a seizure
cards.body:
During a seizure, a person may stiffen, fall and jerk. Stay calm. Your job is to keep them safe until it passes. Note the time it started. Move hard or sharp objects away, put something soft under their head and loosen anything tight around their neck.

Do not hold them down and do not put anything in their mouth. When the jerking stops, check their breathing and place them in the recovery position. Stay with them while they come round, as they may be confused.

Call your local emergency number if it is their first seizure, it lasts more than five minutes, another follows, they are injured, or they do not wake or breathe normally.
cards.apply_it: Learn the five-minute rule: if a seizure lasts longer than five minutes, call for emergency help.

quiz.question: Which of these should you never do during a seizure?
quiz.explanation: Putting objects in the mouth can cause injury or block the airway. Protect the head and time the seizure instead.

cards.title: Recognise a heart attack and a stroke fast
cards.body:
Heart attack signs include chest pain or pressure that may spread to the arms, jaw, neck or back, along with breathlessness, sweating, feeling sick or dizzy. Some people, especially women and older adults, have milder or unusual symptoms. Call your local emergency number straight away, help them sit or rest comfortably and follow the call handler's advice.

For stroke, think FAST. Face: has it drooped on one side? Arms: can they lift both and keep them up? Speech: is it slurred or confused? Time: call your emergency number immediately, even if signs fade.

With both, every minute matters. Note when symptoms began.
cards.apply_it: Teach someone else what FAST stands for today.

quiz.question: In the FAST stroke check, what does the T stand for?
quiz.explanation: T means time: call your local emergency number at once, because fast treatment can limit brain damage.

cards.title: Keep a first-aid kit and take a proper course
cards.body:
A simple kit at home, in the car and at work means you are ready when something happens. Include sterile dressings and plasters of various sizes, bandages, a triangular bandage, disposable gloves, tape, scissors, tweezers, cling film for burns, a foil blanket, and a list of emergency numbers. Check it every few months and replace used or out-of-date items.

Knowing what to do matters even more than having the kit. Reading guides helps, but hands-on practice is what builds the confidence to act. Look for a recognised first-aid course near you; many are short, low-cost or free, and some workplaces pay for them.
cards.apply_it: Check your home first-aid kit today and write a list of anything missing.

quiz.question: What builds the confidence to act in an emergency most effectively?
options: Hands-on practice on a first-aid course
quiz.explanation: Practical training lets you rehearse skills like CPR so you can act calmly when it counts.
